Cogitations
koj-i-TAY-shuns
noun (plural)
From the Latin cogitare, to think or ponder — co, together, and agitare, to turn over. Cogitations are thoughts turned over repeatedly in the mind, deliberate and revolving rather than passing.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, at the close of Daniel’s vision of the four beasts: “Hitherto is the end of the matter. As for me Daniel, my cogitations much troubled me, and my countenance changed in me: but I kept the matter in my heart” (Dan 7:28). Three things are recorded, and each is worth notice. His thoughts much troubled him — the prophet who received the revelation was disturbed by it, which should quiet anyone who imagines that receiving truth from God is a comfortable business. His countenance changed: the trouble was not private but showed in his face, as it did in Belshazzar’s and in Nehemiah’s. And then, “I kept the matter in my heart” — he did not publish his disturbance, discharge it on the nearest listener, or make his own agitation the subject. The etymology is exactly right for what Daniel describes: cogitare is to turn a thing over, and these were thoughts revolving without resolution. Note that Daniel is not rebuked for them. Scripture nowhere requires that the believer feel settled about everything God has shown him. Mary kept all these things and pondered them in her heart; the psalmists ask how long without answer; and Daniel goes on serving under three kings with an unresolved vision turning in his mind.

Webster 1828 Definition

Deep and revolving thoughts; meditations turned over repeatedly in the mind, as Daniel’s after his vision.

COGITATION, n. The act of thinking; thought; meditation; contemplation.

From the Latin cogitare, to think, from co and agitare, to agitate or turn over.

In the plural, the successive or revolving thoughts of the mind.

Purpose or design formed in the mind.

Dan 7:28 is the sole occurrence in the Authorized Version.

Key Scripture

Dan 7:28 — "Hitherto is the end of the matter. As for me Daniel, my cogitations much troubled me, and my countenance changed in me: but I kept the matter in my heart."

Dan 7:15 — "I Daniel was grieved in my spirit in the midst of my body, and the visions of my head troubled me."

Luk 2:19 — "But Mary kept all these things , and pondered them in her heart."

Psa 77:6 — "I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search."

Modern Corruption

Unsettled thoughts are now treated as a condition to be resolved or medicated away, so a believer troubled by what God has shown him concludes something is wrong with his faith.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live distortion is the expectation of settledness. Contemporary religious culture prizes the testimony that resolves, the answer that satisfies, the peace that arrives on schedule; and a Christian whose thoughts keep turning without conclusion is likely to be told he lacks faith, or to conclude it himself. Daniel makes that verdict impossible. He was a man of extraordinary faith — the lions’ den is in the next chapter — and his cogitations much troubled him, visibly, and the book does not say they stopped. What God had shown him about the beasts and the little horn was genuinely disturbing, and being disturbed by disturbing truth is not a failure of grace but a mark of paying attention.

Recover the plain sense: there is a right way to hold an unresolved trouble, and Daniel models it. He kept the matter in his heart — neither denying it nor broadcasting it, neither pretending to a peace he had not been given nor making his agitation everyone else’s business. Mary did the same with things she could not yet understand. Asaph in Psa 77 says his spirit made diligent search and the answer did not come until he remembered the works of the LORD of old. That is the pattern: keep the matter, keep serving, and keep bringing it back to what God has already done. Daniel served under three kings with an unfinished vision turning in his mind, and the vision was true all the while he could not settle it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin cogitare, to turn over — revolving thoughts; Daniel’s trouble after the vision, kept in his heart.

expand to see more

Cogitations — Latin cogitare, from co + agitare, to turn over.

The etymology implies revolving, not passing, thought.

Dan 7:28 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.

Dan 7:15 says his spirit was grieved in the midst of his body.

Compare Luk 2:19, where Mary kept and pondered what she could not yet understand.

Usage

"The prophet who received the revelation was disturbed by it."

"The trouble showed in his countenance and was still kept in his heart."

"Being troubled by disturbing truth is attention, not weak faith."
